newsitem.title: USA: Tornado activity linked to Pacific cooling.
newsitem.headline: Tornado activity linked to Pacific cooling.

text.p: Florida weather researchers said Wednesday they have found a way to forecast periods of unusually heavy tornado activity in the central United States region known as the "tornado belt."

When Pacific Ocean waters off the coast of Peru are colder than normal in the winter, tornado activity the following spring is three to five times greater than normal in the Tennessee and Ohio Valley region, the researchers said.

The phenomenon is dubbed "El Viejo," Spanish for "the old man." It is the flip side of El Nino, "the Christ child" -- the more widely studied Pacific warming pattern that hampers hurricane development in the Atlantic and Caribbean and is linked to flooding and drought in North and South America.

"It's the Dr. Jekyll of El Nino," said Dr. Jim O'Brien, who led the Florida State University team that discovered the tornado link. O'Brien, who was to present the findings in Nashville Wednesday at a climate conference sponsored by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration, said El Viejo was not expected to form this year, a harbinger that next spring will be a quiet one for tornadoes.

El Nino has been linked to a broad range of weather condition changes that affect crops and cause floods in North and South America. O'Brien's study suggests El Viejo's influence may be equally far-reaching.

Like El Nino, El Viejo develops every three to seven years and lasts nine months to a little over a year. El Nino is present when the Pacific waters near the Galapagos Islands off Peru warm to two degrees Fahrenheit above normal. El Viejo occurs when those waters cool to two degrees below normal.
"The last big one this century was in 1988-89," O'Brien said.

In El Viejo years, the dominant air current over the United States is the large, meandering jet stream. It enters the country over the Pacific Northwest, drenching Seattle, and creates another rainband between New Orleans and Cincinnati.
"That allows moist Gulf air to be pumped into the Tennessee-Ohio Valley. It gives you more opportunities for these clashes between the cold Canadian air and the warm, moist air," O'Brien said.

The clashing air masses cause tornadoes to form. "If cold water is happening (off Peru) in the winter then in the following spring you expect to have three times as many tornadoes" in Georgia, Alabama, Tennessee, Kentucky, Ohio, Indiana and Michigan, he said.

Conversely, when El Nino is present, the dominant air current is the subtropical jet stream, which curves across Mexico into the southeastern United States. "It blocks the ability of moist air from the Gulf of Mexico to get up into Oklahoma and Kansas, so they have less tornadoes," he said.

In those years, Texas, Louisiana, Oklahoma, Kansas and Arkansas see fewer tornadoes than in neutral years, when water temperature off Peru are average, the researchers said. They found the link by examining 47 years' worth of tornado records kept by the federal government, mapping out 75-mile square areas of the United States and studying climate factors that affect tornado formation.
Both El Viejo and El Nino result from the ocean's natural rhythms.

"Think about the Pacific Ocean as a big bathtub sloshing back and forth along the Equator. Sometimes when it sloshes it gets warm water in the east. Sometimes when it sloshes it gets cold water," O'Brien said. "It's moving east-west and back. It's also moving up and down."

The up-and-down movement pushes up cold water from the ocean depths, cooling the surface. "The scientific community has been concentrating on the warm side. It's just as easy to have colder water than normal," O'Brien said.
